packs.title: Core ML Cards
packs.blurb: 43 four-choice cards on metrics, data prep, models, validation, and neural nets.

questions.text: What does precision measure for a binary classifier?
questions.rubric: Precision = TP / (TP + FP). Use it when false positives are costly, e.g. spam filters flagging real mail.
questions.answer:
Of everything predicted positive, the share that is actually positive: TP / (TP + FP).
Precision = TP / (TP + FP). Use it when false positives are costly, e.g. spam filters flagging real mail.

options.text: Of all actual positives, the share the model found: TP / (TP + FN).
options.rationale: That is recall, which penalises false negatives.

options.text: The share of all predictions that are correct: (TP + TN) / total.
options.rationale: That is accuracy, which mixes both classes.

options.text: The share of actual negatives correctly rejected: TN / (TN + FP).
options.rationale: That is specificity, the true negative rate.

options.text: Of everything predicted positive, the share that is actually positive: TP / (TP + FP).
options.rationale: Precision penalises false positives, so it answers 'when the model says yes, how often is it right?'.

card.explanation: Precision = TP / (TP + FP). Use it when false positives are costly, e.g. spam filters flagging real mail.

questions.text: A cancer screening model must miss as few sick patients as possible. Which metric do you prioritise?
questions.rubric: When false negatives are expensive (medical screening, fraud catch rate), optimise recall, then keep precision acceptable via the threshold.
questions.answer:
Recall, because it measures the share of actual positives the model catches.
When false negatives are expensive (medical screening, fraud catch rate), optimise recall, then keep precision acceptable via the threshold.

options.text: Precision, because it keeps the positive predictions clean.
options.rationale: Precision ignores missed positives, which is the costly error here.

options.text: Accuracy, because the model should be right as often as possible.
options.rationale: With rare disease, accuracy stays high even when most patients are missed.

options.text: Recall, because it measures the share of actual positives the model catches.
options.rationale: Missing a sick patient is a false negative, and recall = TP / (TP + FN) directly penalises those.

options.text: Specificity, because it tracks how many healthy people are cleared.
options.rationale: Specificity is about negatives; the stated risk is missed positives.

card.explanation: When false negatives are expensive (medical screening, fraud catch rate), optimise recall, then keep precision acceptable via the threshold.

questions.text: What is the F1 score?
questions.rubric: F1 = 2 * P * R / (P + R). Precision 0.9 and recall 0.1 give F1 of 0.18, not 0.5.
questions.answer:
The harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2PR / (P + R).
F1 = 2 * P * R / (P + R). Precision 0.9 and recall 0.1 give F1 of 0.18, not 0.5.

options.text: The arithmetic mean of precision and recall: (P + R) / 2.
options.rationale: An arithmetic mean lets a very high value hide a very low one.

options.text: The harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2PR / (P + R).
options.rationale: The harmonic mean is dragged down by the weaker of the two, so F1 is only high when both are high.

options.text: The share of correct predictions weighted by class frequency.
options.rationale: That describes weighted accuracy, not F1.

options.text: The area under the precision-recall curve.
options.rationale: That is PR-AUC, a threshold-free metric; F1 is computed at one threshold.

card.explanation: F1 = 2 * P * R / (P + R). Precision 0.9 and recall 0.1 give F1 of 0.18, not 0.5.

questions.text: Fraud is 1% of transactions. A model predicts 'not fraud' for everything. What happens to accuracy and F1?
questions.rubric: On imbalanced data, accuracy is misleading. Report F1, PR-AUC, and per-class precision and recall.
questions.answer:
Accuracy is 99%, but F1 for the fraud class is 0 because recall is 0.
On imbalanced data, accuracy is misleading. Report F1, PR-AUC, and per-class precision and recall.

options.text: Accuracy is 99%, but F1 for the fraud class is 0 because recall is 0.
options.rationale: The model never finds a positive, so TP = 0 and both recall and F1 collapse, while accuracy rewards the majority class.

options.text: Accuracy is 1% and F1 is 99%.
options.rationale: Predicting the majority class is correct 99% of the time, so accuracy is high.

options.text: Both are 99% because the model is consistent.
options.rationale: F1 depends on true positives, and there are none.

options.text: Both are 0 because the model is useless.
options.rationale: Accuracy counts true negatives, so it is 99%, not 0.

card.explanation: On imbalanced data, accuracy is misleading. Report F1, PR-AUC, and per-class precision and recall.

questions.text: Which statement about a binary confusion matrix is correct?
questions.rubric: Rows are actual classes, columns are predicted. Always read it before trusting a single summary metric.
questions.answer:
It counts TP, FP, FN and TN, and every threshold-based metric like precision, recall and F1 is derived from it.
Rows are actual classes, columns are predicted. Always read it before trusting a single summary metric.

options.text: It shows the probability the model assigns to each class.
options.rationale: It holds counts of outcomes at a chosen threshold, not probabilities.

options.text: It only applies to multi-class problems.
options.rationale: It works for binary and generalises to N x N for multi-class.

options.text: It is independent of the decision threshold.
options.rationale: Moving the threshold moves counts between cells.

options.text: It counts TP, FP, FN and TN, and every threshold-based metric like precision, recall and F1 is derived from it.
options.rationale: The four cells are the raw counts; the common metrics are just ratios of those cells.

card.explanation: Rows are actual classes, columns are predicted. Always read it before trusting a single summary metric.

questions.text: What does ROC-AUC measure?
questions.rubric: 0.5 is random ranking, 1.0 is perfect. It says nothing about calibration or which threshold to use.
questions.answer:
The probability that a random positive is scored higher than a random negative, across all thresholds.
0.5 is random ranking, 1.0 is perfect. It says nothing about calibration or which threshold to use.

options.text: The accuracy of the model at the 0.5 threshold.
options.rationale: AUC is threshold-free; it summarises all thresholds.

options.text: The share of positives predicted at the best threshold.
options.rationale: That is recall at one threshold, not an area.

options.text: The probability that a random positive is scored higher than a random negative, across all thresholds.
options.rationale: The ROC curve plots TPR against FPR over thresholds; its area is a ranking-quality measure.

options.text: How well predicted probabilities match observed frequencies.
options.rationale: That is calibration; a model can rank well and still be miscalibrated.

card.explanation: 0.5 is random ranking, 1.0 is perfect. It says nothing about calibration or which threshold to use.

questions.text: Positives are 0.5% of the data. Why prefer PR-AUC over ROC-AUC?
questions.rubric: The PR-AUC baseline equals prevalence (0.005 here), so improvements are easier to interpret for rare classes.
questions.answer:
ROC-AUC can look strong because FPR is diluted by the huge negative class; PR-AUC focuses on how clean the positive predictions are.
The PR-AUC baseline equals prevalence (0.005 here), so improvements are easier to interpret for rare classes.

options.text: ROC-AUC cannot be computed on imbalanced data.
options.rationale: It can be computed; it is just optimistic under heavy imbalance.

options.text: ROC-AUC can look strong because FPR is diluted by the huge negative class; PR-AUC focuses on how clean the positive predictions are.
options.rationale: Precision uses FP directly, so thousands of false positives show up in PR even when FPR stays tiny.

options.text: PR-AUC is always higher, so it is easier to report.
options.rationale: PR-AUC is usually lower on imbalanced data; its baseline is the positive rate.

options.text: PR-AUC ignores false positives, which are unimportant here.
options.rationale: Precision is exactly the metric that exposes false positives.

card.explanation: The PR-AUC baseline equals prevalence (0.005 here), so improvements are easier to interpret for rare classes.

questions.text: Your model outputs probabilities. How do you choose the decision threshold?
questions.rubric: Lower the threshold to raise recall, raise it to raise precision. Choose on validation, confirm once on test.
questions.answer:
Pick it on validation data based on the business cost of false positives vs false negatives, not by defaulting to 0.5.
Lower the threshold to raise recall, raise it to raise precision. Choose on validation, confirm once on test.

options.text: Pick it on validation data based on the business cost of false positives vs false negatives, not by defaulting to 0.5.
options.rationale: 0.5 is only optimal when classes and error costs are balanced and probabilities are calibrated.

options.text: Always use 0.5 because probabilities are symmetric.
options.rationale: 0.5 ignores class imbalance and asymmetric costs.

options.text: Tune it on the test set to maximise F1.
options.rationale: Tuning on the test set leaks information and inflates the reported score.

options.text: Threshold does not matter if ROC-AUC is high.
options.rationale: AUC ranks well, but precision and recall still depend on the threshold.

card.explanation: Lower the threshold to raise recall, raise it to raise precision. Choose on validation, confirm once on test.

questions.text: In multi-class classification, what is the difference between macro and micro F1?
questions.rubric: Use macro F1 when rare classes matter; weighted F1 averages per-class F1 by support.
questions.answer:
Macro averages per-class F1 equally; micro pools all TP, FP and FN, so frequent classes dominate.
Use macro F1 when rare classes matter; weighted F1 averages per-class F1 by support.

options.text: Macro is for binary problems, micro is for multi-class.
options.rationale: Both are multi-class averaging schemes.

options.text: Micro weights every class equally regardless of size.
options.rationale: That describes macro averaging.

options.text: They always give the same number.
options.rationale: They diverge whenever class sizes and per-class quality differ.

options.text: Macro averages per-class F1 equally; micro pools all TP, FP and FN, so frequent classes dominate.
options.rationale: Macro exposes weak performance on rare classes, while micro reflects overall volume.

card.explanation: Use macro F1 when rare classes matter; weighted F1 averages per-class F1 by support.

questions.text: When would you prefer MAE over RMSE for a regression model?
questions.rubric: RMSE for costly big misses (e.g. demand spikes), MAE for robust average error. R-squared shows variance explained.
questions.answer:
When you want errors weighted linearly and do not want a few large outliers to dominate the score.
RMSE for costly big misses (e.g. demand spikes), MAE for robust average error. R-squared shows variance explained.

options.text: When you want large errors punished more strongly.
options.rationale: That is the reason to choose RMSE, not MAE.

options.text: When the target is categorical.
options.rationale: MAE and RMSE are for continuous targets.

options.text: When you want errors weighted linearly and do not want a few large outliers to dominate the score.
options.rationale: RMSE squares errors before averaging, so large errors are penalised much more heavily.

options.text: MAE is always better because it is easier to compute.
options.rationale: The choice is about the error cost shape, not computation.

card.explanation: RMSE for costly big misses (e.g. demand spikes), MAE for robust average error. R-squared shows variance explained.

questions.text: Why is log loss (cross-entropy) used to train and evaluate probabilistic classifiers?
questions.rubric: Low log loss means both good ranking and good calibration; it is differentiable, so it works for gradient training.
questions.answer:
It rewards well-calibrated probabilities and heavily penalises confident wrong predictions.
Low log loss means both good ranking and good calibration; it is differentiable, so it works for gradient training.

options.text: It only counts whether the predicted label is correct.
options.rationale: That is 0-1 loss; log loss uses the probability.

options.text: It rewards well-calibrated probabilities and heavily penalises confident wrong predictions.
options.rationale: Loss is -log(p) of the true class, so a confident 0.99 on the wrong class costs far more than an unsure 0.6.

options.text: It is the same as accuracy but faster.
options.rationale: It measures probability quality, not label correctness.

options.text: It is only for regression problems.
options.rationale: Cross-entropy is the standard classification loss.

card.explanation: Low log loss means both good ranking and good calibration; it is differentiable, so it works for gradient training.

questions.text: Which is an example of data leakage?
questions.rubric: Fit every preprocessing step on train only, ideally inside a Pipeline so each CV fold refits it.
questions.answer:
Fitting a StandardScaler on the full dataset before splitting into train and test.
Fit every preprocessing step on train only, ideally inside a Pipeline so each CV fold refits it.

options.text: Fitting a StandardScaler on the full dataset before splitting into train and test.
options.rationale: The scaler learns test-set mean and variance, so test performance is no longer an honest estimate.

options.text: Scaling features after the train/test split using train statistics.
options.rationale: This is the correct way to avoid leakage.

options.text: Using cross-validation for model selection.
options.rationale: Cross-validation is a guard against overfitting, not leakage by itself.

options.text: Dropping a feature with many missing values.
options.rationale: Dropping a column does not pass future or test information into training.

card.explanation: Fit every preprocessing step on train only, ideally inside a Pipeline so each CV fold refits it.

questions.text: A churn model uses 'account_closed_date' as a feature and scores 0.99 AUC. What is likely wrong?
questions.rubric: Ask for every feature: would I know this value at the moment I make the prediction?
questions.answer:
Target leakage: the feature is only known after churn happens, so it will not exist at prediction time.
Ask for every feature: would I know this value at the moment I make the prediction?

options.text: The model is simply excellent and ready to ship.
options.rationale: Near-perfect scores on a hard problem usually signal leakage.

options.text: The dataset is too small.
options.rationale: Size does not explain a feature that directly reveals the label.

options.text: The model needs more regularisation.
options.rationale: Regularisation does not fix a feature that should not be available.

options.text: Target leakage: the feature is only known after churn happens, so it will not exist at prediction time.
options.rationale: A feature that encodes the outcome makes offline metrics look perfect and fails in production.

card.explanation: Ask for every feature: would I know this value at the moment I make the prediction?

questions.text: How should you handle missing values in a numeric feature?
questions.rubric: Also check why data is missing; for time series or sensor data, interpolation or forward-fill can be better.
questions.answer:
Impute with a train-fitted statistic like the median, and optionally add a 'was missing' indicator feature.
Also check why data is missing; for time series or sensor data, interpolation or forward-fill can be better.

options.text: Always drop every row with any missing value.
options.rationale: This can throw away much of the data and bias the sample.

options.text: Fill with the mean computed over train and test together.
options.rationale: Using test statistics is leakage.

options.text: Impute with a train-fitted statistic like the median, and optionally add a 'was missing' indicator feature.
options.rationale: Median is robust to outliers, and the indicator preserves the signal that missingness itself may carry.

options.text: Replace missing values with zero in every case.
options.rationale: Zero may be a meaningful value and distort the distribution.

card.explanation: Also check why data is missing; for time series or sensor data, interpolation or forward-fill can be better.

questions.text: How do you handle outliers before training a linear model?
questions.rubric: Tree models are robust to outliers in features; linear and distance-based models are not.
questions.answer:
Investigate them first, then cap, transform (e.g. log), or use a robust loss depending on whether they are errors or real extremes.
Tree models are robust to outliers in features; linear and distance-based models are not.

options.text: Always delete everything beyond two standard deviations.
options.rationale: Blind deletion removes real rare events and biases the model.

options.text: Investigate them first, then cap, transform (e.g. log), or use a robust loss depending on whether they are errors or real extremes.
options.rationale: Real extremes carry signal; data-entry errors should be fixed or removed.

options.text: Outliers never matter for linear models.
options.rationale: Squared-error losses are very sensitive to outliers.

options.text: Scale the features and outliers disappear.
options.rationale: Standard scaling keeps outliers as outliers.

card.explanation: Tree models are robust to outliers in features; linear and distance-based models are not.

questions.text: A 'country' feature has 200 categories. Which encoding choice is reasonable for a linear model?
questions.rubric: Trees tolerate ordinal encoding better; for high cardinality, consider out-of-fold target encoding or embeddings.
questions.answer:
One-hot encoding, possibly grouping rare categories into 'other' to limit sparsity.
Trees tolerate ordinal encoding better; for high cardinality, consider out-of-fold target encoding or embeddings.

options.text: One-hot encoding, possibly grouping rare categories into 'other' to limit sparsity.
options.rationale: One-hot avoids implying an order; grouping rare levels reduces noise and dimensionality.

options.text: Label encoding as 0..199, because it keeps one column.
options.rationale: Integers imply a false order and distance for linear models.

options.text: Drop it, because categorical features cannot be used.
options.rationale: Categoricals carry signal once encoded.

options.text: Target encoding computed on the full dataset.
options.rationale: Target encoding must be fit out-of-fold on train or it leaks the label.

card.explanation: Trees tolerate ordinal encoding better; for high cardinality, consider out-of-fold target encoding or embeddings.

questions.text: Which models usually need feature scaling?
questions.rubric: StandardScaler for roughly normal features, MinMax for bounded ranges, RobustScaler with outliers.
questions.answer:
Distance and gradient-based models like k-NN, SVM, logistic regression with regularisation, and neural networks.
StandardScaler for roughly normal features, MinMax for bounded ranges, RobustScaler with outliers.

options.text: Decision trees and random forests.
options.rationale: Tree splits are threshold-based and invariant to monotonic scaling.

options.text: No model needs scaling.
options.rationale: Distance-based and regularised models clearly do.

options.text: Only models with categorical features.
options.rationale: Scaling is about numeric ranges.

options.text: Distance and gradient-based models like k-NN, SVM, logistic regression with regularisation, and neural networks.
options.rationale: Unscaled features let large-range columns dominate distances and slow gradient descent.

card.explanation: StandardScaler for roughly normal features, MinMax for bounded ranges, RobustScaler with outliers.

questions.text: Which is a sound first approach to a 1:100 class imbalance?
questions.rubric: Resampling belongs inside the training fold only. Threshold tuning is often as effective as resampling.
questions.answer:
Use stratified splits, class weights or resampling on train only, and evaluate with PR-AUC, F1 and recall.
Resampling belongs inside the training fold only. Threshold tuning is often as effective as resampling.

options.text: Oversample the whole dataset with SMOTE before splitting.
options.rationale: Synthetic samples leak into the test set and inflate scores.

options.text: Ignore it; accuracy will reflect true performance.
options.rationale: Accuracy is dominated by the majority class.

options.text: Use stratified splits, class weights or resampling on train only, and evaluate with PR-AUC, F1 and recall.
options.rationale: Handling imbalance changes training; honest evaluation needs untouched test data and the right metrics.

options.text: Delete features until classes balance.
options.rationale: Features do not change class proportions.

card.explanation: Resampling belongs inside the training fold only. Threshold tuning is often as effective as resampling.

questions.text: Which is good feature engineering for predicting car prices?
questions.rubric: Good features encode domain knowledge; always check they exist at prediction time.
questions.answer:
Derive vehicle age from registration year, mileage per year, and brand-model groupings, fit on train data.
Good features encode domain knowledge; always check they exist at prediction time.

options.text: Add the listing's final sale price as a feature.
options.rationale: That is the target itself, which is leakage.

options.text: Derive vehicle age from registration year, mileage per year, and brand-model groupings, fit on train data.
options.rationale: Domain-derived features expose relationships the raw columns hide, like depreciation over age.

options.text: Add random noise columns to increase dimensionality.
options.rationale: Noise features only add variance.

options.text: Convert every numeric feature to text.
options.rationale: That removes the numeric structure models can use.

card.explanation: Good features encode domain knowledge; always check they exist at prediction time.

questions.text: What does logistic regression model?
questions.rubric: Strengths: fast, interpretable coefficients, good baseline. Limit: needs feature engineering for non-linear patterns.
questions.answer:
The log-odds of the positive class as a linear function of the features, passed through a sigmoid to get a probability.
Strengths: fast, interpretable coefficients, good baseline. Limit: needs feature engineering for non-linear patterns.

options.text: The log-odds of the positive class as a linear function of the features, passed through a sigmoid to get a probability.
options.rationale: It is a linear classifier with probabilistic output, trained with log loss.

options.text: A continuous target as a straight line.
options.rationale: That is linear regression.

options.text: A tree of if-else splits.
options.rationale: That is a decision tree.

options.text: Only multi-class problems via voting.
options.rationale: It is natively binary; softmax regression extends it to multi-class.

card.explanation: Strengths: fast, interpretable coefficients, good baseline. Limit: needs feature engineering for non-linear patterns.

questions.text: Training error is low, validation error is much higher. What does this indicate?
questions.rubric: Fix variance with more data, regularisation, simpler models, or early stopping. Fix bias with richer features or models.
questions.answer:
High variance (overfitting): the model memorises training data and does not generalise.
Fix variance with more data, regularisation, simpler models, or early stopping. Fix bias with richer features or models.

options.text: High bias (underfitting).
options.rationale: Underfitting shows high error on both training and validation.

options.text: The model is well balanced.
options.rationale: A big gap means it is not.

options.text: The validation set is too large.
options.rationale: Validation size does not create a systematic gap.

options.text: High variance (overfitting): the model memorises training data and does not generalise.
options.rationale: A large train-validation gap is the classic overfitting signal.

card.explanation: Fix variance with more data, regularisation, simpler models, or early stopping. Fix bias with richer features or models.

questions.text: What is the difference between L1 and L2 regularisation?
questions.rubric: Lasso = L1, Ridge = L2, Elastic Net = both. Stronger penalty means more bias, less variance.
questions.answer:
L1 adds the absolute weights and can push some to exactly zero (feature selection); L2 adds squared weights and shrinks them smoothly.
Lasso = L1, Ridge = L2, Elastic Net = both. Stronger penalty means more bias, less variance.

options.text: L1 increases model complexity and L2 decreases it.
options.rationale: Both reduce complexity by penalising weights.

options.text: L2 produces sparse models with many zero weights.
options.rationale: L2 shrinks weights but rarely makes them exactly zero.

options.text: L1 adds the absolute weights and can push some to exactly zero (feature selection); L2 adds squared weights and shrinks them smoothly.
options.rationale: The L1 penalty has corners at zero, which produces sparse solutions.

options.text: They only apply to decision trees.
options.rationale: They are penalties on model weights, typical for linear models and nets.

card.explanation: Lasso = L1, Ridge = L2, Elastic Net = both. Stronger penalty means more bias, less variance.

questions.text: How does a random forest reduce overfitting compared to a single deep tree?
questions.rubric: Random forests are strong defaults: little tuning, robust to outliers, give feature importance.
questions.answer:
It averages many trees trained on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets, which reduces variance.
Random forests are strong defaults: little tuning, robust to outliers, give feature importance.

options.text: It trains trees sequentially, each fixing the previous errors.
options.rationale: That is boosting, not bagging.

options.text: It averages many trees trained on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets, which reduces variance.
options.rationale: Bagging plus feature randomness decorrelates the trees, so averaging cancels their individual errors.

options.text: It prunes a single tree to depth one.
options.rationale: That describes a decision stump.

options.text: It uses a linear model at every leaf.
options.rationale: Standard random forests use constant leaf predictions.

card.explanation: Random forests are strong defaults: little tuning, robust to outliers, give feature importance.

questions.text: How does gradient boosting build its model?
questions.rubric: XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost usually win on tabular data; tune learning rate, depth, trees, and use early stopping.
questions.answer:
It adds shallow trees sequentially, each fitted to the residual errors (gradients) of the current ensemble.
XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost usually win on tabular data; tune learning rate, depth, trees, and use early stopping.

options.text: It adds shallow trees sequentially, each fitted to the residual errors (gradients) of the current ensemble.
options.rationale: Each step moves the prediction in the direction that reduces the loss, scaled by a learning rate.

options.text: It trains many independent trees in parallel and averages them.
options.rationale: That is bagging, as in random forests.

options.text: It trains one very deep tree and prunes it.
options.rationale: Boosting uses many weak learners.

options.text: It clusters the data and fits a model per cluster.
options.rationale: That is not how boosting works.

card.explanation: XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost usually win on tabular data; tune learning rate, depth, trees, and use early stopping.

questions.text: When would you pick a random forest over gradient boosting?
questions.rubric: In interviews: bagging reduces variance, boosting reduces bias.
questions.answer:
When you want a robust baseline with little tuning and less risk of overfitting noisy data.
In interviews: bagging reduces variance, boosting reduces bias.

options.text: When you need the highest possible accuracy on clean tabular data.
options.rationale: Tuned boosting usually wins there.

options.text: When the data is images.
options.rationale: Neither is the default for raw images; CNNs are.

options.text: Random forests cannot overfit at all.
options.rationale: They overfit less, but not never.

options.text: When you want a robust baseline with little tuning and less risk of overfitting noisy data.
options.rationale: Boosting often scores higher but is more sensitive to hyperparameters and noise.

card.explanation: In interviews: bagging reduces variance, boosting reduces bias.

questions.text: What is a key limitation of k-means?
questions.rubric: Pick k with the elbow method or silhouette score; use DBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and noise.
questions.answer:
You must choose k up front, and it assumes roughly spherical, similar-sized clusters.
Pick k with the elbow method or silhouette score; use DBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and noise.

options.text: It requires labelled data.
options.rationale: k-means is unsupervised.

options.text: It cannot handle more than two features.
options.rationale: It works in any dimension.

options.text: You must choose k up front, and it assumes roughly spherical, similar-sized clusters.
options.rationale: k-means minimises within-cluster squared distance to centroids, which favours round clusters.

options.text: It always finds the global optimum.
options.rationale: It can converge to local optima; use multiple initialisations.

card.explanation: Pick k with the elbow method or silhouette score; use DBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and noise.

questions.text: Why might a tree model beat logistic regression on tabular data?
questions.rubric: Start with a logistic baseline for interpretability, then compare with gradient boosting.
questions.answer:
Trees capture non-linear effects and feature interactions without manual feature engineering.
Start with a logistic baseline for interpretability, then compare with gradient boosting.

options.text: Trees always need less data.
options.rationale: Deep trees can need a lot of data to generalise.

options.text: Trees capture non-linear effects and feature interactions without manual feature engineering.
options.rationale: Logistic regression is linear in its features unless you add interactions yourself.

options.text: Logistic regression cannot output probabilities.
options.rationale: It outputs probabilities natively.

options.text: Trees are always more interpretable than linear models.
options.rationale: A single tree is readable, but ensembles are not.

card.explanation: Start with a logistic baseline for interpretability, then compare with gradient boosting.

questions.text: Which task is unsupervised learning?
questions.rubric: Supervised = labels (regression, classification); unsupervised = no labels (clustering, dimensionality reduction).
questions.answer:
Grouping customers into segments without any labels.
Supervised = labels (regression, classification); unsupervised = no labels (clustering, dimensionality reduction).

options.text: Grouping customers into segments without any labels.
options.rationale: Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data, like clusters.

options.text: Predicting house prices from past sales.
options.rationale: That is supervised regression.

options.text: Classifying emails as spam using labelled examples.
options.rationale: That is supervised classification.

options.text: Detecting cars in images using annotated boxes.
options.rationale: That is supervised object detection.

card.explanation: Supervised = labels (regression, classification); unsupervised = no labels (clustering, dimensionality reduction).

questions.text: What is the role of each split?
questions.rubric: Typical split 70/15/15; use cross-validation instead of a fixed validation set when data is small.
questions.answer:
Train fits parameters, validation selects models and hyperparameters, test gives one final unbiased estimate.
Typical split 70/15/15; use cross-validation instead of a fixed validation set when data is small.

options.text: Test is used to tune hyperparameters, validation for the final score.
options.rationale: The roles are reversed.

options.text: Validation is optional if the training score is high.
options.rationale: A high training score says nothing about generalisation.

options.text: All three can share rows to save data.
options.rationale: Shared rows leak information across splits.

questions.text: What does k-fold cross-validation give you?

questions.text: Which tuning approach is usually more efficient than a full grid search?

questions.text: What is an embedding in ML?

options.rationale: One-hot is sparse and carries no similarity.

options.text: A dense vector representation where similar items (words, documents, images) are close in vector space.
options.rationale: Embeddings let you compare meaning with distance measures like cosine similarity.
